The Yellowfin hind (Cephalopholis hemistiktos) is a moderately sized serranid that attains an ultimate total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters] based on records from the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf. A comprehensive life-history study, conducted at a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], revealed that the age at birth, corresponding to the hatching period of the pelagic eggs, is 12 days [ab = 12 days]. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are minute, with their wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.00045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00045 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 0.95 millimeters documented for this species. This endotrophic larval stage relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that occurs shortly after mouth opening and retinal differentiation. The early life stages of C. hemistiktos thus exhibit a rapid developmental pace typical of many tropical epinephelines, with hatching occurring just under two weeks following fertilisation under these controlled thermal conditions.

Field surveys conducted across coral reef habitats in the western Indian Ocean have provided robust estimates of the size at which Yellowfin hind undergo sexual maturation. The total length at puberty for this species is 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters], a threshold that marks the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively viable organism. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight regressions applied to specimens from these surveys, is 69 grams [Wwp = 69 grams]. This mass is attained during the sub-adult phase, typically after a period of several months of rapid post-settlement growth on the reef. Individuals below this size are exclusively immature, and the onset of gonadal recrudescence becomes histologically evident only once this body size is approached, indicating a size-driven rather than strictly age-driven reproductive strategy. The consistency of this benchmark across several populations suggests that it represents a fundamental life-history constraint for the species.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of adult female Yellowfin hind was measured. Under the same thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], field-caught specimens showed a GSI of approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%]. This value, which is comparable to those reported for the congeneric species Cephalopholis cyanostigma, suggests a moderate reproductive effort consistent with an iteroparous, multiple-batch spawning strategy typical of many groupers. The measurement was taken from gravid individuals during the peak reproductive months, ensuring that the index captured the maximal gonadal investment prior to spawning events. Such data are crucial for understanding the energetic trade-offs between basic physiological costs and gamete production, particularly in a species that inhabits the fluctuating thermal environments of shallow coastal waters.

The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass, has been modelled from length-weight relationships established for Cephalopholis hemistiktos across its geographic range. The maximum recorded body mass in adults is 622 grams [Wwi = 622 grams], a figure that corresponds well with the species' modest body plan among the Epinephelinae. This mass is typically achieved by older individuals that have completed their somatic growth phase, and it is corroborated by numerous captures of large, presumably senescent, specimens. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty of 69 grams [Wwp = 69 grams] represents only about eleven percent of the ultimate attainable mass, indicating a substantial scope for post-maturation growth. This pattern is common among long-lived, slow-growing serranids, where reproductive maturity precedes the attainment of maximum size by a considerable margin, allowing individuals to channel energy toward both somatic increase and annual spawning events over many years.

Longevity records for the Yellowfin hind, compiled from tag-recapture studies and validated by otolith increment analysis, indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of 26 years [am = 26 years] when assessed at the prevailing water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This considerable life span places C. hemistiktos among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait that confers resilience to variable recruitment conditions but also renders the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing. The species' modest adult body plan, with an ultimate total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], combined with its pronounced longevity, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises survival and iterative reproduction over rapid generational turnover. As a protogynous hermaphrodite, older and larger individuals, which are predominantly female, contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the population over decades, a demographic structure that demands cautious management in artisanal fisheries throughout its distribution.
